chunks: What motors and solenoids are, and uses. The question: What is a motor/solenoid? What can they be used for?
A motor turns electrical energy into spinning motion. A solenoid turns it into a short push or pull in a straight line. Both are built from a coil of wire.
When current flows through the coil, it makes a magnetic field, and that field makes a force.
Motors are used for anything that spins or drives, and solenoids for things like locks and valves.
Picture a door lock. A solenoid is like a little piston: switch it on and it snaps a bolt a few millimeters, switch it off and a spring pushes the bolt back.
A motor is more like a wheel that keeps being pushed around. Electromagnets give the pushes, and as the wheel turns, the pushes are timed so they keep going in the same direction.
Electrical model of a brushed DC motor: coil resistance R, coil inductance L, and a back-EMF source E proportional to speed (orange).
A solenoid is the same circuit without the speed-dependent E (its inductance changes as the plunger moves instead).
Everything about startup current, steady-state current and flyback follows from this one loop.
Actuator: a device that turns an electrical signal into motion or force. Coil: many turns of wire. Current in it makes a magnetic field.
Plunger: the movable iron rod inside a solenoid that the field pulls in.
Brushed DC motor: a simple motor that uses brushes and a commutator (a switch that turns with the shaft) to keep the current direction right as it spins.
Inductive load: a load made of a coil, which resists sudden changes in current ("What is inductance?")
Think of a 12 volts door-lock solenoid whose coil has 24 ohms of resistance. By Ohm's law the current is 12 over 24 equals 0. 5 amps, which is 6 watts.
Switch it on and the plunger pulls the bolt. Switch it off and a spring returns it.
A small fan motor on the same 12 volts supply would instead spin continuously, and it would draw less current once it is up to speed than when it starts. That is the whole idea.
"A motor converts electrical energy into rotation and a solenoid converts it into a short linear push or pull, both using a coil that creates a magnetic field.
A solenoid is a coil with a movable plunger and a spring, good for locks, valves and relays.
A motor has coils on a rotor in a magnetic field, so current produces torque, used for fans, pumps, wheels and drones.
Electrically both are inductive loads, a resistance in series with an inductance, and a motor also produces a back-EMF."
